title: GPU OOM + CUDA/driver mismatch debug notes
content:
Context:
- Repro on dedicated node: g4dn-like instance (NVIDIA T4), Ubuntu 20.04, Docker.
- Workload: batched text-generation using transformer model (lm-v2, ~7B) with fp16.
- Intermittent: sometimes runs fine, sometimes fails with OOM or driver/kernel errors after warmup.

Symptoms observed (2025-11-10 through 2026-02-24):
- Immediate crash in some containers: "CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version".
- Frequent runtime OOM when multiple models loaded concurrently: "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 1.02 GiB (GPU 0; 15.90 GiB total capacity; 12.35 GiB already allocated)".
- Occasional kernel-level errors: "cuda runtime error (98): unspecified launch failure" or "no kernel image is available for execution on the device".
- dmesg shows occasional GPU page faults and driver recovery messages.

Commands run (copy/paste from investigation):
- Check GPU and driver:
  nvidia-smi -q -d PIDS,UTILIZATION,MEMORY
  -> shows driver 470.57.02 on some hosts, 525.85.12 on others. Memory usage fluctuates.

- Check CUDA toolkit/compiler in container:
  nvcc --version  # in some images not present
  python -c \"import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.is_available())\"
  -> examples: '2.1.0+cu118', '11.8', True  OR '2.0.1+cu117', '11.7', True

- Inspect container base image labels:
  docker inspect --format '{{.Config.Labels}}' my-image:latest
  grep -i cuda /etc/os-release || true

- Memory introspection during run: added prints: 
  import torch;
  print('cuda_total:', torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory)
  print(torch.cuda.memory_allocated(), torch.cuda.memory_reserved())

- Run reproduction with isolated device: 
  CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python reproduce.py --batch-size 1 --use-fp16

- Recreated environment on dev machine (same docker image) -> no failure for hours.

Error snippets collected:
- "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 2.00 GiB (GPU 0; 15.90 GiB total capacity; 13.05 GiB already allocated; 512.00 MiB free; 12.44 GiB reserved in total by PyTorch)"
- "CUDA error: unrecognized error code 30" (seen once during stress test)
- "CUDA runtime error (35): CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version"
- From dmesg: "NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:00:1e.0): 79, pid 12345, ch 00000020, intr 10000000. Xid 79 generally indicates a fault handled by the driver (possibly a kernel bug or invalid memory access)."

Hypotheses / notes:
1) Driver vs runtime mismatch across fleet: some nodes upgraded drivers (525+), some left at 470. Containers built against cu118 (requires newer drivers) may run on newer-driver hosts but fail on older-driver hosts with "driver insufficient".
   - Evidence: container image labels show cu118; failing hosts report driver 470 -> known incompatibility.

2) Memory fragmentation/reservation by previous processes: long-lived processes that allocate VRAM and don't release (or reserved by CUDA context) lead to effective free memory being less than reported.
   - Evidence: torch.cuda.memory_reserved() sometimes very large even after del + torch.cuda.empty_cache().

3) Mixed CUDA/CuDNN versions at runtime due to host libs shadowing container libs (mounted libs from host into container or LD_LIBRARY_PATH misconfigured).
   - Evidence: some nodes have /usr/local/cuda symlink pointing to 11.4 while container expects 11.8; observed multiple /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libcudnn.so.* versions.

4) Tensor cores / JIT kernel mismatch for Turing vs Ampere architectures causing "no kernel image is available for execution on the device" when image built targeting sm_80 but device is sm_75. Some containers compiled with GPU arch flags.
   - Evidence: error "no kernel image is available for execution on the device". Node type mismatch possible if mixed fleet sizes.

5) NCCL/infiniband or driver bug under high load causing GPU resets (Xid 79).

Actions taken so far (with results):
- Pinned nodes to driver >= 515 on rollout -> reduced "driver insufficient" errors on new runs. (partial fix)
- Rebuilt container images with cu117 and cu118 variants and added explicit runtime checks at startup:
  python -c \"import torch, sys; print(torch.version.cuda); sys.exit(0 if torch.version.cuda.startswith('11.8') else 1)\"
  -> image now fails fast if runtime mismatch.
- Added startup probe to node agent to check nvidia-smi driver >= required and prevent scheduling of incompatible images.
- Added periodic process scan on nodes to kill orphan processes hogging GPU (heuristic). Helped reduce fragmentation but not eliminate.
- For OOMs: introduced per-model memory limit and guard rails (max_batch_tokens, lower prefetched KV cache size). Reduced incidence but still appears under concurrency.

Remaining open troubleshooting steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Collect full env dump from failing host when issue reproduces: nvidia-smi -q, ldconfig -p | grep cuda, ls -l /usr/local/cuda*, ldd on libtorch.so inside container. Attach to jira-INFR-3421.
- [ ] Reproduce locally with synthetic concurrent clients to simulate fragmentation pattern. Script: stress_gpu.py (TODO: parameterize concurrency, alloc pattern).
- [ ] Run kernel debug / enable persistence mode + watchdog to capture gdb traces if driver recovers (hard). Coordinate with infra/SRE.
- [ ] Confirm that we never mount host /usr/local/cuda into containers by accident (search deployment templates).
- [ ] Add early startup guard in runtime: check driver compatibility (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=driver_version --format=csv,noheader) vs image CUDA ABI table and refuse to serve if mismatch.
- [ ] Consider shifting to distributing container variants by GPU architecture (labels: turing, ampere) and driver version. Scheduler should honor tags.

Temporary mitigation checklist (what we applied):
- Block scheduling of cu118 images to hosts with driver < 515.
- Restart long-running model processes nightly to release CUDA contexts. (crude but effective short-term)
- Enable smaller default per-request cache size and reduce max batch size for problematic models.

Notes for Jordan / Liam:
- Jordan: can you add ldconfig/ldd checks to the node startup agent? Quick script idea under /opt/redwood/bin/gpu-env-check.sh.
- Liam: can you try reproducing with 3 concurrent model loads on a clean node (driver 525) and then drop driver to 470 (simulate) to observe failure modes? Record all outputs.

Short term troubleshooting commands to run on failing host (put in runbook):
1) nvidia-smi -q > /tmp/gpu-$(date +%s).txt
2) docker ps -q | xargs -r -I{} sh -c 'docker inspect {} --format "{{.Name}} {{.Image}}"' > /tmp/docker-list.txt
3) for c in $(docker ps -q); do docker exec $c bash -lc "python -c 'import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.version.cuda, torch.cuda.device_count())'" >> /tmp/containers-torch.txt; done
4) dmesg | grep -i NVRM > /tmp/nvrm.txt
5) LD_LIBRARY_PATH check: for c in $(docker ps -q); do docker exec $c bash -lc 'echo $LD_LIBRARY_PATH' >> /tmp/ldpaths.txt; done

Contextual reminders / gotchas:
- CUDA runtime version reported by torch/version may be the build-time CUDA (e.g., cu118) even if host driver supports newer runtimes; still need driver >= minimum ABI.
- Some GPUs (T4) need driver >= specific version for compute capability optimizations when using newer cuDNN/cuda libs.
- Emptying cache in PyTorch is not always enough if contexts from previous processes persist. Need to ensure process exit + driver context cleared.

Endnotes / next steps summary:
- Primary blocking item: fleet driver heterogeneity -> implement node gating + image tagging so images run only on compatible drivers.
- Secondary: memory fragmentation under concurrency -> add process lifecycle controls and better scheduler-level packing to avoid noisy neighbors.
- Follow up with SRE to run a controlled experiment: one host where we intentionally alternate driver versions and run stress tests, capture Xid traces.

Attachments in ticket: snippets of nvidia-smi outputs, dmesg Xid 79 logs, docker inspect outputs (attached to jira:INFR-3421).

-- Maya
